title: Skill in Speech
note: He defines this as being able to say the words that carry a minister’s work to the end he intends. It expands “speak with certainty” from K634, so it follows the chapter on the minister.

couplets.plain: To have the good called a good tongue is a good not found among any other goods.
couplets.pm: The quality ministers can’t do without is what the wise call the good of the tongue. Even in others it isn’t counted among other goods, but stands above them. Ministers must bring the world under them, so they need it as a thing apart. If even those with no work of parting and joining need it, those who have that work surely do.

links.quote: a good not found among any other goods
links.reason: Ranks a good tongue as a good apart from every other.

couplets.plain: Gain and ruin both come from it, so guard carefully against any slip in your speech.
couplets.pm: Rise and ruin for their ruler and his kingdom come from what ministers say, so they must guard against any lapse in speech. Good words bring gain and bad words ruin, yet both are speech. A lapse by others harms few, but theirs falls on all living beings at once, so he says “guard carefully”.

links.quote: guard carefully against any slip in your speech

couplets.plain: Speech is that which holds its hearers fast, and is said so that even those who haven’t heard it long for it.
couplets.pm: For ministers, true speech seeks the qualities that bind those who took them as friends, and is said so that even enemies drop their enmity and want friendship. Those qualities are freedom from error, brevity, clarity, sweetness and great use. He rejects reading தகையவாய் as “being worthy”, a plural that can’t go with the singular மொழிவது.

links.quote: Speech is that which holds its hearers fast
links.reason: Sets the test of true speech: it binds those who hear and draws even those who haven’t.

couplets.note: கேட்டார் and கேளார் are those who heard and those who haven’t in the plain reading. He takes them as those who accepted you as friends and those who didn’t, your enemies.

couplets.plain: Know the right way and speak your words. No righteousness and no wealth is greater than that.
couplets.pm: Ministers should speak knowing their own standing and their hearers’, the differences that come from birth, learning, conduct, wealth, looks and age, and address each as is fitting. Nothing brings more righteousness and wealth. It is righteousness because it keeps step with the world and pleases, and wealth because it gets their work done.

links.quote: Know the right way and speak your words

couplets.plain: Say your word only when you know that no other word can beat it.
couplets.pm: Say the word you have in mind once you know that no word can defeat it. The other word is a rival’s contrary word, and to defeat is to surpass in quality. So speak so that yours wins. Some read this as “speak so that there is no equal word and no better word”.

links.quote: no other word can beat it

couplets.plain: To speak so that others want to hear, and to take what is useful from what others say, is the way of the flawless.
couplets.pm: When you speak to others, speak so that they want to hear more. When they speak to you, take the use of their words and leave the rest. That is the settled way of those without fault in a minister’s calling. They don’t scorn others’ words even if they have flaws, because scorning those less able doesn’t suit the able.

links.quote: speak so that others want to hear
links.reason: Joins making others want to hear with taking the use of what they say, as the way of the flawless.

couplets.plain: A man who speaks well, never slips and has no fear is hard for anyone to beat in a contest.
couplets.pm: One who can say what he has in mind so that others accept it, even against their interest, who forgets no point however many there are, and who isn’t afraid: no one can beat him in a dispute. No rival can win against a man with these three qualities by splitting his allies or drawing them away.

couplets.plain: The world quickly does as it is asked, if it finds those who can speak in good order and sweetly.
couplets.pm: If you find those who can set out what is to be said in order, and sweetly, the world quickly accepts it. Order means knowing what comes first and what after. Sweetness means pleasing the hearers. A Sanskrit saying has it that one in a hundred thousand can speak well, so he says “if it finds”.

links.quote: The world quickly does as it is asked

couplets.plain: Those who don’t know how to say a few flawless words surely desire to say many.
couplets.pm: Those who don’t know how to say a few faultless words in this way want to gather many. Some prize speaking at length without a pause as skill. He says “surely” to insist that only those who can’t speak in this way do that, and the able don’t.

links.reason: Holds up a few flawless words as the mark the long-winded miss.

couplets.plain: Those who can’t unfold what they have learned so that others grasp it are like flowers that bloom in clusters but have no scent.
couplets.pm: Those who can’t explain the books they have learned so that others understand are like flowers that bloom in a cluster but have no scent. A flower in full bloom without scent isn’t worn, and one who has studied but can’t speak isn’t held in esteem.

links.quote: can’t unfold what they have learned
flowers that bloom in clusters but have no scent
